title: I Let the Community Bagel-Kettle Clock Catch the Baker Who Cut the List

parts.text: I dropped dough at 4:04 a.m. and baker Rye was already boiling past our numbered list. The slate said: ONE KETTLE. FORTY MINUTES. DOZEN FOLLOWS THE LIST. I was twenty-eight, kitchen volunteer, holding a boil card that listed our batch. Rye shrugged. "Bakers are the kettle." I photographed the slate, the list, and his dozen on our skimmer. Then I asked for the kettle log. At 4:12 the kitchen pinged why Rye's name was on our forty. I kept my voice kitchen-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A slate is only a slate until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen can see Rye's dozen on our skimmer during our boil.

social.video_title: He boiled past our numbered list on our kettle — Part 1/2
social.description: Bagel kettle, a baker on our skimmer, a forty-minute slate he posted. I logged the dozen. Would you have asked for the kettle log?

parts.text: Rye called it a float until the kitchen asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the slate, and the dozen still. The kettle went back to our list. Rye ran his own forty and told the next baker atmosphere was always about chew. Chew is a word bakers use when a list exists. Kettle policy now has a second line: BAKERS ARE NOT THE KETTLE. I keep our card on a labeled clip. Rye brown-bags his jokes. The kitchen finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Kettle log, numbered list, and a second line on the slate. Was a float ever our skimmer?
